idea: An app where campus event organizers post leftover food and students get notified to come grab it. Two of us, part-time (~12h/week each), 8 weeks, $300 budget. Must be free for students. Want a live map and push notifications.

nodes.label: Campus leftover-food sharing app
Organizers post leftover food (photo, location, pickup window)
nodes.rationale: Must-have: the supply side of the app

nodes.label: Student feed of available food
nodes.rationale: Students need one place to see what's available now

nodes.label: Push notifications for new food posts
nodes.rationale: Must-have: food goes fast, so students need to know immediately

nodes.label: SMS alerts for students without the app
nodes.rationale: Reaches students who won't install an app

objections.reason: Validate demand before adding a paid notification channel.
The added cost is not justified before validating demand for another alert channel.
Validate demand before spending much of the budget on SMS.

nodes.label: Live map of food locations
nodes.rationale: User asked for it; makes finding food in unfamiliar buildings easy

objections.reason: A live map adds substantial work without being necessary for the pilot; use the text-location variant instead.

nodes.label: Building and room shown as text, with a link to campus maps
nodes.rationale: Smaller variant of the live map: most of the value for 2h

nodes.label: Claim / reserve a portion
nodes.rationale: Prevents wasted trips when food is gone

objections.reason: Reservations add coordination work and are not necessary to test whether the core sharing flow works.
Defer reservations to make room for pilot feedback and automatic expiry without exceeding capacity.

nodes.label: In-app chat between organizers and students
nodes.rationale: Questions like 'is there any vegan food left?'

objections.reason: Chat adds moderation and privacy work that is not needed to validate the core flow.
Chat adds moderation and privacy complexity beyond the pilot's needs.
Chat is not essential to test the core posting and discovery flow and adds moderation work.

nodes.label: Campus email sign-in
nodes.rationale: Keeps the app to the campus community and deters abuse

nodes.label: Free for students
Allergen and dietary labels required on every post
nodes.rationale: Students with allergies must be able to decide safely

nodes.label: Food-safety liability (time since prepared, handling)
nodes.rationale: Posting checklist plus a pickup-window limit and disclaimer

nodes.label: Students may not trust food from strangers
nodes.rationale: Show the posting organization's name and verified campus email

evidence.title: Consumer food waste behaviour in universities: Sharing as a means of prevention
evidence.summary: A campus food-sharing intervention ran into barriers: trust, people's visceral relationship with food, and norms about acceptable food sources.

nodes.label: Hosting and domain
Which organizations will post first?
Show allergen information as organizer-provided; allow unknown and warn that information is not independently verified
nodes.rationale: Avoid giving students false confidence when allergen information is incomplete or unverified.

nodes.label: Push notifications require student opt-in
nodes.rationale: Respect student choice and avoid unsolicited notifications.

nodes.label: Pilot with campus organizers and gather student feedback
nodes.rationale: Validate that organizers will post and students find the feed useful before expanding scope.

nodes.label: Automatically expire food posts when their pickup window ends
nodes.rationale: Prevents stale listings and reduces wasted student trips.

negotiation.message: On r1-architect: Accept: it preserves the live map, push, and claims while adding secure backend foundations and post expiry, with the workload still within capacity.

On r1-delivery: Reject: text directions and a lean pilot are practical, but deferring the live map and claims removes too much of the requested product value while leaving considerable capacity unused.

On r1-evidence: Reject: the allergen caveat, opt-in, and pilot feedback improve safety and validation, but deferring the live map sacrifices a distinctive requested feature; those safeguards could be added without dropping it.

On r1-architect: The backend foundation and automatic expiry are useful, but a live map, claims, push, and sign-in in 124 hours leave only about 10 hours of capacity buffer. The combination creates too much delivery risk for this timeline.

On r1-delivery: This keeps the must-have posting and push features while replacing the costly live map with simple directions and deferring claims and chat. The ample schedule buffer makes a working pilot more likely, though backend foundations and notification opt-in should be addressed.

On r1-evidence: This preserves the lean pilot scope and adds practical safeguards for unverified allergen information, opt-in notifications, and early user validation. Those additions reduce rollout risk without consuming much of the available capacity.

On r1-architect: I could accept this plan: it preserves the required features and adds backend access rules and post expiry, which help reliability. I prefer it to the current plan, though the map-and-claims scope is ambitious and allergen uncertainty, notification opt-in, and pilot validation remain unaddressed.

On r1-delivery: I could accept this lean pilot: text directions are a practical substitute for a live map, and required features and food-safety measures remain. I prefer it to the current plan, but would want allergen uncertainty and push opt-in made explicit, plus a way to validate organizer and student demand.

On r1-evidence: This is my preferred candidate: it preserves the required core, avoids false confidence in organizer-provided allergen information, requires push opt-in, and includes a focused pilot to test whether organizers post and students find the feed useful. Text directions are a reasonable lower-cost first version while the live map remains deferred.

No candidate was accepted by everyone. r1-evidence has the most support (2/3) and becomes the draft for the next round. Tie broken by Nash bargaining product (balance of every agent's margin above its minimum): r1-evidence 0.0080, r1-delivery 0.0020, r1-architect 0.0007.

The text-location pilot is a reasonable fallback, but with only 58% of capacity planned it leaves enough room to deliver the live map the user asked for, alongside claims that prevent wasted trips. I recommend activating both and adding automatic expiry so old food listings do not linger. (Changed because: The measured plan shows only 78 of 134.4 available hours planned, making it clear that the requested live map and useful claims feature can fit without exceeding capacity.)
negotiation.counteroffer: Keep the pilot foundation, add the live map and claims, and automatically expire posts at the end of their pickup window; this totals about 128 hours against 134.4 available.

negotiation.message: On r2-architect: Accept: it delivers the requested live map, push notifications, and useful claim and expiry behavior within available capacity. The schedule is tight, so keep the map implementation bounded to campus locations.
On r2-evidence: Expiry is a worthwhile improvement, but leaving the requested live map disputed retains only the text-and-link fallback and weakens the product’s distinctive value.
On r2-architect: I would not commit the pilot to the full live map and claims: they add implementation and integration risk, and 128 planned hours leaves too little buffer for a reliable launch.

On r2-evidence: Automatic expiry is a modest, practical improvement that helps avoid stale listings without taking on the live map and claims. The schedule is tight, but this is a manageable addition for the pilot.

On r2-architect: Acceptable because it retains opt-in notifications, organizer-provided allergen warnings, and adds expiry while delivering the requested map. Claims and the map add scope with only about six hours of remaining capacity; confirm claimed portions and availability can be updated, and monitor schedule risk.

On r2-evidence: Prefer this safer, more deliverable first release: it adds expiry and retains the text location/link alternative without taking on the full map and claims. The summary says to activate the pilot, but the resulting plan still leaves it proposed; make organizer and student feedback an actual delivery task so the value assumptions are tested.

No candidate was accepted by everyone. r2-architect has the most support (2/3) and becomes the draft for the next round. Tie broken by Nash bargaining product (balance of every agent's margin above its minimum): r2-architect 0.0066, r2-evidence 0.0048.
